entries.clue: Long and hard, being gently stimulated all round (7)

indicatorNotes.stimulated: Something stimulated has been stirred into movement, and letters stirred up do not come back in the order they were given.
indicatorNotes.all round: All round says the shuffled letters are laid right the way around the outside of the letter already named.

blocks.note: the six letters of gently in another order, ready to wrap round
h is the standard short form for hard, the grade stamped on a pencil

annotation.surface: Somebody staying long and hard under gentle attention.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Long and hard' looks like one phrase describing the answer, yet only 'Long' defines it and 'hard' is a single letter hiding at the end of the pair.
annotation.definitionFit: Lengthy is the adjective for something of great length, a plain synonym for long with a hint of too much of it.

entries.clue: Unmoved, just like Trump crushing Republicans? (10)

indicatorNotes.crushing: To crush a thing is to press in on it from every side, so what is crushed finishes up inside the word doing the crushing.

blocks.note: imperious is the standing charge against him: high-handed and expecting to be obeyed
R is the standard short form for Republican, the letter printed after an American politician's name

annotation.surface: Trump steamrollering his own party without turning a hair.
annotation.walkthrough: This one does not add up, and the fault is the setter's: the R of Republicans was meant to go inside IMPERIOUS, but the answer carries a V in that slot. Cyclops owned up to the slip once the puzzle was published.
annotation.definitionFit: Something impervious lets nothing through, so a person impervious to pressure is left unmoved by it.

entries.clue: Balls dropped? Just the opposite, causing shock (4)

indicatorNotes.Just the opposite: The opposite of a word as written is that word read the other way about, back to front.

blocks.note: balls are nuts, and NUTS is taken here from its last letter to its first

annotation.surface: A crude enquiry about whether somebody's testicles have descended, met with a flat contradiction.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark sells 'Balls dropped?' as locker-room talk, which is all the cover the wordplay needs. 'Just the opposite' points at direction, not at disagreement.
annotation.definitionFit: To stun someone is to shock them into stillness, which is the verb sense of shock.

entries.clue: Ridicule ten getting pissed in pub (6)

indicatorNotes.getting pissed: Pissed is British for drunk, and a drunk loses hold of the proper order of things, letters included.
indicatorNotes.in: In names the place, so the letters just named go inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: a bar is a pub, and it splits to take the other letters in
the three letters of ten in another order

annotation.surface: Mocking ten drinkers as they get steadily drunk in the pub.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pissed' is British for drunk rather than angry, and drunkenness is the standard reason letters come out in the wrong order. Ten stays a number all through, which is why it reads as people.
annotation.definitionFit: Banter is teasing talk at somebody's expense, ridicule in its lighter and more sociable form.

entries.clue: Cares halved at first? Doubtful (2,3,5)

indicatorNotes.at first: At first fixes a position, putting the piece it stands beside at the front instead of where the clue names it.

blocks.note: to halve a thing is to cut it in two
he cares = he minds, as in 'I don't mind'

annotation.surface: Somebody's concern apparently cut in half at the outset, which seems unlikely.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cares' is the verb minds, as in 'I don't mind', rather than a noun about worries. Being in two minds is hesitation between two options, not feeling things by halves.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody in two minds cannot settle on either option, which is what calling them doubtful says.

entries.clue: Tip: Labour leader needed inside prompt (4)

indicatorNotes.leader: A word's leader is the letter out in front of it, so that opening letter is the only one taken.
indicatorNotes.needed inside: Inside names the position, so the letter just named is dropped into the middle of the word that follows.

blocks.note: a cue is the prompt an actor waits for
the front letter of Labour

annotation.surface: A tip-off that Labour's leader is the man wanted in the prompt corner.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Labour leader' reads as a politician and amounts to the letter L. 'Prompt' is the theatre noun, not the adjective for quick.
annotation.definitionFit: A clue is what points you towards an answer, the same service a tip does.

entries.clue: Crew with US enforcement, very dangerous in the main (4,3)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the answer instead of replacing it: pack ice is a thing rather than a quality, and the setter names it by the hazard it presents and the place it is found.

blocks.note: a pack is a crew or gang, as in a pack of thieves
ICE is Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the American agency that detains and deports migrants

annotation.surface: A gang working hand in glove with American immigration officers, dangerous for the most part.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In the main' reads as 'mostly' and means at sea, the main being an old word for the open ocean. ICE became familiar outside America through Trump's deportation raids.
annotation.definitionFit: Pack ice is sea ice driven together into one shifting mass, the stuff that crushes a hull, and 'the main' is the open sea.

entries.clue: Malice spreads anytime leader is kicked out (6)

indicatorNotes.spreads: What spreads goes off in all directions, and letters sent in all directions do not stay in the order given.
indicatorNotes.leader: The leader of a word is the letter at its head, which fixes which letter the clue is about to lose.
indicatorNotes.is kicked out: Being kicked out is being thrown clear altogether, so that letter takes no part in what is left.

blocks.note: anytime once its opening letter has gone, the six that get shuffled
the front letter of anytime, the one thrown out

annotation.surface: Spite breaking out whenever a leader is thrown out of office.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Anytime' is a word here rather than a stretch of time, and 'leader' is its A rather than any person. The sacking in the surface is the deletion the wordplay wants.
annotation.definitionFit: Enmity is settled ill will between people, malice seen as a standing state rather than a passing impulse.

entries.clue: Bush gets Trump backers to import northern crude oil (8)

indicatorNotes.to import: To import is to bring something in from outside, so what follows is carried inside the word before it.
indicatorNotes.crude: Crude means unrefined, and unrefined letters have not yet been put into their proper order.

blocks.note: MAGA, from Make America Great Again, is what Trump's supporters wear and call themselves
n is the standard short form for northern
the three letters of oil in another order

annotation.surface: A Bush getting Trump's base to bring in crude oil from the north.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bush' is a shrub and is planted first so that a president comes to mind instead. 'Crude oil' is the neat part: crude is the shuffling word and half the surface's cargo at once.
annotation.definitionFit: The magnolia is a flowering shrub or small tree, so bush is the general class the answer belongs to.

entries.clue: see 25dn.
Maybe Polanski goes on strike to secure undeveloped land (5,4)

blocks.note: Zack Polanski has led the Green Party of England and Wales since 2025, so he is one Green that 'maybe' can stand for
to belt somebody is to strike them

annotation.surface: A party leader walking out on strike to save open country from the builders.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Strike' is the verb belt, not the picket line the surface builds around it. Polanski is a Green by party rather than by name, which is why 'Maybe' is there.
annotation.definitionFit: The green belt is the ring of protected open country round a British city, which planning law keeps unbuilt.

entries.clue: (&13ac.) Vow a hacker made about what Trump's actions do (5)

indicatorNotes.made about: Made about says the letters were put together afresh rather than left standing in the order they arrive in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

annotation.walkthrough: 'About' does two jobs: the vow is about Trump in the surface and the letters are moved about in the wordplay. Splitting the phrase over two entries keeps either half from looking like English.
annotation.definitionFit: Havoc is devastation and to wreak it is to bring it about, the phrase English keeps for damage done at scale.

entries.clue: see 12ac.

blocks.note: to cap something is to restrict it, as with a pay cap
it has stood for sex since the 1920s and the original It girl
the A-list is the top rank of celebrity

annotation.surface: Putting a limit on sex with somebody famous.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Celebrated' points at the list the famous are ranked on rather than at anyone standing on it. A capitalist need not be rich, which is what the question mark concedes.

entries.clue: Pence joins Democrats in America – oddly a potential life-saver (9)

indicatorNotes.oddly: Oddly means strangely, and letters put together strangely are not in the arrangement they were handed over in.

blocks.note: p is the short form for pence, the British coin
D after an American politician's name marks a Democrat
anagram fodder, seven letters

annotation.surface: Mike Pence crossing the floor to sit with American Democrats.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pence' is the coin, not Trump's first vice-president, and that swap is the whole trap. 'Oddly' is a shuffling word rather than a comment on the politics.
annotation.definitionFit: A paramedic is the ambulance crew member trained to keep a casualty alive before hospital, so saving a life is the potential named.

entries.clue: "Un-Republican" march – Commander-in-Chief covers arse (10)

indicatorNotes.covers: To cover a thing is to lie over it on every side, so the letters named afterwards sit inside the ones named before.

blocks.note: a protest march is a demo, short for demonstration
the post is written C-in-C, which gives these three letters
a rat and an arse are both names for a contemptible person

annotation.surface: A march against the Republicans at which the Commander-in-Chief covers for some lowlife.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Covers arse' is the political idiom for protecting a colleague, and the mechanics want it literally instead. C-in-C is the American president's other title.
annotation.definitionFit: American politics offers only two parties, so what is not Republican is Democratic, and the quotation marks own up to that shorthand.

entries.clue: "Old boiler": can that be PC? (6)

blocks.note: before washing machines, the week's laundry was boiled up in a big metal tub that took its name from the metal
PC stands for police constable, and this is the nickname every British cop show uses for one

annotation.surface: Wondering aloud whether calling an elderly woman an old boiler is acceptable language.
annotation.walkthrough: 'PC' is the police constable while the surface wants politically correct, the same two letters serving both. Cyclops gets the insult and the apology into six words.
annotation.definitionFit: A copper is the copper tub laundry was once boiled in, and copper is also the everyday British word for a police officer.

entries.clue: Pictures of Chirac in email content (6)

indicatorNotes.content: What is content is what a thing holds, so the answer is sitting inside these words rather than being built from their meanings.

blocks.note: the letters run across the words, the c closing Chirac and in ema finishing the run

annotation.surface: Photographs of the late French president turning up in somebody's inbox.
annotation.walkthrough: The pictures is the British name for the cinema, a usage fading since the multiplex arrived. Jacques Chirac was president of France from 1995 to 2007.
annotation.definitionFit: Going to the pictures is the older British way of saying going to the cinema.

entries.clue: Military unit in Pacific – oh, or Tehran (6)

indicatorNotes.in: In says the answer is lying inside the words that follow rather than being assembled out of them.

blocks.note: the letters run across four words, from the end of Pacific to the start of Tehran

annotation.surface: Wondering whether a regiment is posted in the Pacific or perhaps Tehran.
annotation.walkthrough: A cohort was one tenth of a Roman legion, which is why the word still sounds military. The dash and the 'oh' make the hiding place read as somebody thinking aloud.
annotation.definitionFit: A cohort was a division of the Roman army, so military unit names it exactly.

entries.clue: Smear last of oil inside tool (7)

indicatorNotes.last of: The last of a word is its closing letter, so only that one letter is taken.
indicatorNotes.inside: Inside names the position, so the letter goes into the middle of the word that follows.

blocks.note: a sander is the power tool that smooths wood
the closing letter of oil

annotation.surface: Working the last drop of oil around the inside of a tool.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Smear' is the newspaper sense, an attack on somebody's reputation, rather than anything to do with oil. Spoken it is slander; printed it would be libel.
annotation.definitionFit: A smear is an untrue story put about to damage somebody, which is what slander is when spoken aloud.

entries.clue: A number of thumbs up Trump's behind – tens perhaps? (7)

indicatorNotes.perhaps: Perhaps says the word is not quite what it claims to be, so its letters are taken in some other arrangement.

blocks.note: ass is the American word for the part he sits on
the four letters of tens in another order

annotation.surface: Thumbs stuck up Trump's backside, ten of them perhaps.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface asks to be read as one crude image, which hides the join between definition and wordplay. 'Behind' is the noun for a backside, not a word about position.
annotation.definitionFit: An assent is an act of agreement, and a raised thumb is how agreement gets given without speaking.

entries.clue: Cryptic clue's too hard – fail to keep up (4,5)

indicatorNotes.Cryptic: Something cryptic is deliberately disguised, and the plainest disguise for a set of letters is to print them out of order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
h is the standard short form for hard, joined to the fodder

annotation.surface: A solver grumbling that a cryptic clue is beyond them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cryptic' reads as a description of the clue in front of you and is the shuffling instruction. The H is the hard of pencil grades, the same H that turns up all over this puzzle.
annotation.definitionFit: To lose touch is to fall out of contact or out of step with something, which is failing to keep up with it.

entries.clue: Holding power, what Thatcher wouldn't do for a boost (6)

indicatorNotes.Holding: To hold a thing is to have it within your grasp, so what is held sits inside the word doing the holding.

blocks.note: Thatcher told the 1980 Tory conference 'the lady's not for turning', refusing the U-turn on economic policy her critics wanted
p is the standard short form for power

annotation.surface: Thatcher in office, refusing the one change of course that might have lifted the economy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Holding power' reads as her grip on office and asks only for a single letter. The U-turn she would not perform is the shape of the word itself.
annotation.definitionFit: An upturn is a rise in trade or fortunes after a slump, the boost a struggling economy waits for.

entries.clue: Beats members' wear (5)

blocks.note: to sock somebody is to hit them hard
a member is a limb in the old sense, and these go on the feet

annotation.surface: The clothing worn by the members of some club.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Members' is the limb sense and socks go on the feet, while Cyclops leaves you thinking of another member entirely. Both halves of the clue are definitions, with nothing to assemble.
annotation.definitionFit: To sock somebody is to hit them, so socks are beats; and socks are worn on the feet, which are members in the old sense of limbs.

entries.clue: Party leader finally beaten by international set (5)

indicatorNotes.finally: Finally points at the end of the word beside it, so only that last letter is taken.

blocks.note: the closing letter of beaten
i is the standard short form for international
a liquid sets into a gel, as hair gel does

entries.clue: (&10dn.)You'll be dead unlucky when he comes at you with his long tool (4)

annotation.definition: You'll be dead unlucky when he comes at you with his long tool

entries.clue: Wind up getting temperature one time, on wearing fur (9)

indicatorNotes.on wearing: What is worn goes round the wearer, so the fur named here is wrapped about the letters it has on.

annotation.walkthrough: 'Wind up' is the business sense, closing a company or a meeting down, not anything to do with clockwork. Ermine is worn rather than named in Britain's grandest robes.

entries.clue: Trouble-makers backing politician's intrusion into lives (4)

indicatorNotes.backing: Something backing is travelling the other way, so its letters are read from the end to the start.

annotation.definitionFit: An imp is a small mischievous devil, and the word has long served for anybody bent on causing trouble.

entries.clue: State agent is into working? My arse! (8)

indicatorNotes.into: Into names a destination, so the letters before it are set inside the ones that follow.
indicatorNotes.working: Working a material is kneading it about, and letters worked like that do not keep the order they started in.

blocks.note: the six letters of my arse in another order
the two letters of is, taken as they stand

annotation.surface: Somebody scoffing at the notion that a government agent is keen on hard work.
annotation.walkthrough: 'My arse!' is the British expression of flat disbelief, and Cyclops wants its letters as well as its tone. 'Into' is the instruction to insert rather than the surface's enthusiasm.
annotation.definitionFit: An emissary is somebody sent out by a government to carry its business abroad, which is what state agent names.

entries.clue: Over-indulged Post Office is covered in mud (6)

indicatorNotes.covered in: Being covered in something means it is all around you, so these letters go inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: silt is the fine mud a river drops

annotation.surface: A Post Office branch left plastered with river mud.
annotation.walkthrough: The Post Office collects Cyclops's mud after the Horizon scandal, in which hundreds of sub-postmasters were wrongly prosecuted over faulty accounting software. 'Over-indulged' is the child sense of the answer, not the milk one.
annotation.definitionFit: A spoilt child is one given too much of its own way, which is what over-indulged describes.
